title: Pushing Real-Time Updates
summary: Start with polling; add SSE or WebSockets only when the product needs a live connection.
keyPoints: Polling is the simplest real-time mechanism and is often fast enough.
SSE streams server-to-client events over HTTP and reconnects with an event ID.
WebSockets are bidirectional and stateful, so they need connection-aware scaling.
Publish through a fan-out layer instead of making one gateway the message router.
Per-conversation sequence numbers turn reconnect into a replay problem.
Bound every per-connection buffer; slow clients must resync, not grow memory without limit.

complexity.note: Freshness is capped by the interval.

complexity.time: held until an event or timeout
complexity.note: Works through most proxies but reconnects per update.
Bidirectional with the lowest per-message overhead.
Large rooms need sharded topics or read-time merge.

commonMistakes: Opening a WebSocket for a feature that only needs a five-second poll.
Treating the socket as the source of truth and losing messages when a client disconnects.
Round-robining long-lived connections and ending up with uneven gateway load.
Queuing every update for a slow client until the gateway runs out of memory.
interviewNotes: Ask how fresh the data must be before choosing a transport.
Say whether the connection is one-way or bidirectional and whether it must survive reconnects.
Name the connection registry and where it lives.
Explain resume with sequence numbers or Last-Event-ID, plus the snapshot fallback.
Say what is allowed to drop: presence and typing yes, chat messages no.

checkYourself.question: When is SSE a better fit than a WebSocket?
checkYourself.answer: When updates flow only from server to client, such as notifications, live scores, or progress. SSE reuses HTTP, reconnects automatically, and avoids a custom bidirectional protocol.

checkYourself.question: Why do persistent connections make load balancing harder?
checkYourself.answer: A connection stays pinned to one server, so connect-time round robin can leave capacity uneven and a server failure forces all of its clients to reconnect.

checkYourself.question: How does a reconnecting client avoid missing messages?
checkYourself.answer: It sends the last sequence number or event ID it processed. The server replays from that point, or sends a fresh snapshot if the gap is too large.
